title: Whole-Body Motion Guided Reference Generation for Uncertainty-Aware Compliant Assistance
authors: Muyuan Ma; Long Cheng; Lijun Han; Haotian Zhai; Xinpan Meng; Xiuze Xia; Houcheng Li; Zeyu Liu
abstract: Exoskeletons have shown great potential for augmenting human physical capabilities, yet generating reliable assistance remains challenging because human motion patterns and interaction requirements vary substantially in practice. To address this problem, a dual-loop assistance strategy is proposed to couple multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation with variable admittance control, where trajectory variance links the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop controller. The generator synthesizes future exoskeleton trajectories through denoising, primarily using whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. To reduce cross-modal representation mismatch, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize the human motion encoder, the exoskeleton proprioception encoder, and the trajectory generator. In the inner loop, multiple future trajectories are sampled from the generator to estimate the trajectory mean and variance. The mean is used as the control reference, while the variance provides an uncertainty measure for prediction reliability. This measure is further incorporated into a stiffness regulation law, enabling compliant assistance with input-to-state stability under bounded lumped interaction input. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces muscle activation levels compared with standard baselines, while also decreasing users' metabolic energy expenditure relative to the unassisted condition.

title: RaSFNet: Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network for LiDAR Semantic Segmentation
authors: Chuang Chen
abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.

title: RankAlign: Vision-Language Representation Alignment via Rank Transformation
authors: Enzhe Zhao; Marco Fiorucci; Lamberto Ballan
abstract: While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that vision and language models converge toward compatible latent geometries, recovering class-level correspondences between unpaired modalities without cross-modal supervision remains challenging. Existing relational matching methods compare within-modality similarity kernels directly, although the same semantic structure may be represented through different numerical parameterizations across modalities. We propose RankAlign, a rank-based normalization strategy for class-level unpaired vision-language matching. RankAlign transforms each within-modality similarity kernel into an ordinal relational representation before permutation matching, while leaving the correspondence space and matching solver unchanged. The resulting representation is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations of similarity values while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching. We provide exact-recovery and stability guarantees that characterize correspondence recovery under both exact and partial ordinal agreement. Experiments across diverse frozen vision and language encoders and multiple datasets demonstrate improved and more stable class-level correspondence recovery, including under label corruption and domain shift.

title: Constraint Reasoning and Large Language Models Join Forces: Providing Contrastive Explanations for Real-World Optimisation-Based Applications
authors: Roger X. Lera-Leri; Filippo Bistaffa; Athina Georgara; Juan A. Rodríguez-Aguilar
abstract: We focus on optimisation-based Decision Support Systems in real-world applications. In this context, we aim to provide contrastive explanations that answer users' questions about recommendations based on the solution of an optimisation problem, specifically a Mixed-Integer Program (MIP). Addressing this endeavour is crucial to ensure human oversight of the decisions implemented, as required by international guidelines on trustworthy and responsible automated decision-making systems. We propose a novel methodology that combines constraint reasoning techniques and Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate contrastive explanations for optimisation problems encoded as MIPs. Although LLMs have shown impressive capabilities in Natural Language processing, they can produce incorrect answers due to reasoning limitations. To overcome these limitations, we leverage constraint reasoning techniques to distil the information necessary to produce an explanation, which is then passed as input to an LLM as the so-called graph of reasons. Such a graph captures the semantics and the relationships among constraints of the optimisation problem. Results on real-world scheduling domains show that incorporating constraint reasoning improves explanations generated by the LLM. In particular, using the graph of reasons enables the LLM to produce natural-language explanations that include more relevant reasons while reducing errors compared to explanations generated without this structure.

title: A General-Purpose Dual-Path Interaction Framework for Multi-View Medical Image Segmentation: Alleviating Data Volume Dependency in Small-Sample Regimes
authors: Shuhuan Wang; Yuanyuan Cui; Pengju Wang; Huimin Guo; Ling Yue; Yin Gu; Yanchao Zhang; Wei Feng; Yunhe Liu; Wei Qian; Mingjun Xu; Shuang Liu; He Ma
abstract: The performance of medical image segmentation depends on a large amount of annotated data, and most segmentation models experience a significant drop in performance in low-sample-size scenarios. Existing semi-supervised and weakly supervised methods rely on specific network architectures, while traditional multi-view-assisted segmentation methods require strictly paired samples, which limits their clinical applications. To address these issues, we propose DPIF, a general-purpose plug-and-play dual-path interaction framework compatible with arbitrary encoder-decoder segmentation networks, which leverages cross-view anatomical complementarity to reduce annotation reliance. DPIF first performs Sinkhorn optimal transport-based cross-view distribution alignment to establish global semantic correspondence without sample-level pairing. It then adopts conditional mutual information-guided feature decoupling to enable bidirectional knowledge transfer only within the shared semantic space, suppressing view-specific noise. Finally, persistent homology-based topological regularization encodes anatomical invariants as unsupervised priors to mitigate overfitting. Experiments were conducted using 24 baseline models on a private multicenter echocardiography dataset and two public datasets. The results show that DPIF-enhanced models outperform single-view baseline models when trained on comparable amounts of data. Notably, most dual-path variants trained on 40\% - 60\% of the data achieve performance comparable to that of single-view models trained on the full dataset. This demonstrates that DPIF provides a general-purpose and scalable solution for data-scarce multi-view medical image segmentation problems.

title: Hierarchical Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment via Dynamic Granularity Discovery and Optimal Transport
authors: Pengfeng Song; Shaozhong Zhang; Pengfei Shao
abstract: Fine-grained image-text retrieval requires a model not only to assess global semantic consistency between an image and a text, but also to model visual evidence for local textual semantics, including objects, attributes, quantities, actions, and relations, so as to distinguish semantically similar candidates. Existing methods commonly use fixed image patches, detected regions, or text tokens as the basic matching units and then aggregate local interactions through max pooling, cross attention, or similarity accumulation. Such strategies remain limited in semantic unit construction and global matching consistency. This paper proposes a hierarchical fine-grained cross-modal alignment framework, termed HFCMA. The framework progressively transforms low-level patch and token representations into adaptive visual regions and textual phrases, and then performs structured region-phrase matching within a global retrieval scoring process. Specifically, HFCMA first adopts dynamic granularity discovery (DGD) to aggregate raw patches and tokens into semantically compact visual regions and textual phrases. It then formulates region-phrase matching as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem, thereby estimating a structured alignment matrix under global marginal constraints. To reduce background noise and local semantic drift, HFCMA further introduces background debiasing, textual importance weighting, and prototype consistency regularization. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO show that HFCMA effectively combines dynamic semantic unit construction with OT-based structured matching under a dual-encoder retrieval framework. The resulting fine-grained score provides structured local alignment information for candidate ranking and improves the discrimination of subtle semantic differences.

title: Query-Time Calibration of CLIP Features for Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
authors: Dominik Engel; Yousef Rajeh; Leon Sick; Ivan Viola
abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.

title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Hayat; Jahangir Baig; Shayan Ahmed; Ahmed Faraz Ayubi
abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

title: Data Representation at Scale: Extracting Meaningful Knowledge from Massive Datasets
authors: Ylenia Galluzzo
venue: Nova Science Publishers (Nova Science Publishers, Inc.)
abstract: From genomic sequence analysis to real-time sustainability monitoring, and from medical decision support to neurophysiological signal processing, Big Data meaningful knowledge extraction boosts scientific discovery and societal progress. Large-scale biological sequences reveal information about living organisms, while IoT sustainability data show how socio-environmental systems work. Clinical and imaging data support surgery planning, while EEG signals provide insights into cognitive processes. From a computational perspective, these heterogeneous sources share a common issues: transforming raw, high-dimensional, and noisy observations into structured representations that are both machine learning-ready and semantically meaningful.This PhD thesis proposes novel knowledge extraction techniques from heterogeneous and large-scale data, integrating distributed Big Data infrastructures, vector and graph-based representations, and machine learning methods ranging from classical approaches to deep learning. Heterogeneous input data, time series, images, biological sequences, and text, are processed through novel frameworks for meaningful feature extraction and embedding, producing structured latent representations Z ∈ RN×d that support statistical and predictive analysis of learned features in all domains and, in the sustainability domain, a knowledge graph that encodes relational structure between entities.Four application domains are considered: Biological data, Neurophysiological data, Sustainability data, and Medical data. For Biological data, the focus is on analyzing genomic sequences and constructing compact sequence representations that combine two complementary components: a distributed Burrows–Wheeler Transform (BWT) index, providing compressed and searchable access to large sequence collections, and the BioSet2Vec framework, devoted to the extraction of compact and statistically significant k-mer dictionaries that characterize biological sequence sets. With respect to Neurophysiological data, the aim is to extract neural signatures from EEG signals as cognitive knowledge representations. In the Sustainability context, there is modeling of stakeholder relationships via knowledge graphs and real-time energy monitoring via edge–cloud analytics. Lastly, for Medical data multimodal surgical decision support in reductive mastoplasty is addressed via probabilistic fusion of clinical and meaningful morphometric representations.

title: Self-Referential Fibration Well 1: The Arithmetic Hierarchy of Equivalence Problems—Sharpening the Decision Complexity of Categorical Fiber Towers
authors: changzheng zhou; ziqing zhou
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In the standard recursion-theoretic framework, this paper gives layer-by-layerarithmetic-hierarchy readings for object-equivalence decision problems on a stratified family of sets. The stratified carrier is taken to be a recursively enumerablestructure family: the membership predicate for level-n objects is Σn (level 0 consistsof total recursive sets, level 1 the usual W-sets, and level 2 Σ2-sets). Equivalence istaken to be extensional equality of objects, and a witness of non-equivalence is takenin negative form. This paper proves that the prenex form of the non-equivalence witness problem NEQn is Σn+1, and that the prenex form of the equivalence problemEQn is Πn+1; by an m-reduction construction, NEQn is Σn+1-complete and EQn isΠn+1-complete for all n ≥ 0. The inter-level embedding gives NEQn ≤m NEQn+1;a reverse reduction does not exist, since otherwise it would force Σn+2 ⊆ Σn+1,contradicting the strictness of the hierarchy; hence the hierarchy tower is strictlymonotone. Two boundary cases are treated explicitly: the completeness statementat level 0 is given relative to total-function indices over the domain D0, and thenon-equivalence witness is an unbounded existential search rather than a boundedcheck; the prefix of the cofinite-set problem COF is ∃∀∃, its correct anchor is NEQ2,and COF cannot be reduced to the Σ2-complete NEQ1. This paper further registers the semantic bifurcation caused by the choice of carrier: each upward stepof the set-family tower corresponds to one level of complexity, while the Kleenehigher-order functional tower yields, by quantifier counting, a Π2n upper bound oftwo levels per stage, but this reading is a counting reading rather than a completeness claim. The isomorphism variant involves second-order existential quantifiersin the encoding of function graphs, and its faithful landing point is on the analytichierarchy side Σ1; the coordinates of the arithmetic tower do not cover this variant;object isomorphism obtains a Σn+2-type arithmetic count only under the restrictedreading of finite sets or effective bijections. The main result of this paper belongsto the tower of extensional equality of objects; the level count and completenessdirection of the morphism-equivalence tower are registered as open problems.

title: The Medieval Text and the Modern Question: AI for Multilingual Semantic Retrieval across Centuries
authors: Antoni Mestre
abstract: Multilingual access to medieval literature requires retrieval systems to bridge historical and cross-lingual semantic variation. This article introduces HistRAG, a language-aware framework combining lexical retrieval, multilingual dense representations, historical adaptation, hybrid fusion, and cross-encoder reranking. HistRAG separates the effects of document modernization, query adaptation, and retrieval architecture within a unified experimental setting. The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous collection of Medieval Catalan literature using equivalent queries in three contemporary languages. Results show that lexical retrieval is highly sensitive to query language, while multilingual dense representations provide more robust cross-lingual access. Fixed hybrid fusion offers no systematic advantage over dense retrieval, and historical adaptations produce heterogeneous, non-additive effects. Cross-encoder reranking achieves the strongest average effectiveness, although its contribution varies across languages and evaluation subsets. These findings support an architecture- and language-sensitive approach to semantic retrieval from historically distant collections and provide a reproducible basis for extending AI-enabled access to other medieval textual traditions.

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
authors: Neel Dey; Adrian V. Dalca
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. We use our 3D foundation model, anatomix, to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes and further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific, component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system placed first on the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at https://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
authors: Yang Luo; Tiantian Ji; Zifeng Kang; Yucheng Wang; Yong Liu; Zhiyi Yin; Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).

title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
authors: Zongsheng Li; Shengyuan Zhu; Zimo Zhang; Hanyao Li; Shengming Wang; Quanying Liu
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

title: More Interactions Make Communications More Efficient: A Directed Information Bottleneck Approach to Task-Oriented Communication
authors: Zhirun Zheng; Yiqin Deng; Phone Lin; Yuguang Fang
abstract: Task-oriented communication improves communication efficiency by transmitting semantic information required for downstream tasks, but may incur redundancy with previously transmitted information. To address this issue, we propose a variational directed information bottleneck joint source-channel coding (VDIB-JSCC) framework that transmits only previously unacquired information. Specifically, we use directed information to characterize the causal flow of task-relevant incremental information and theoretically demonstrate its advantages over mutual information and conditional mutual information. Based on this metric, we formulate a directed information bottleneck (DIB) objective that balances task-relevant information preservation and redundant information compression. We further derive a variational formulation, termed VDIB, whose tractable upper bound serves as the training loss. The encoder integrates a Vision Transformer for frame-wise semantic extraction and a Mamba-based causal state-space model for capturing temporal dependencies and extracting incremental information, while the decoder uses a Mamba-based state-space model for task inference. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 video streams demonstrate that VDIB-JSCC achieves higher classification accuracy with less transmitted information than state-of-the-art semantic communication methods. These results show that leveraging historical knowledge enables task completion with less information, improving communication efficiency.

title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
authors: Junming Liu; Marcel Böhme
abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.

title: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset
authors: Mohammad Abolnejadian; Matthew Brehmer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset 📄 Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3830398.3830522💻 Code: https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast Supplemental dataset for the paper: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings Mohammad Abolnejadian and Matthew Brehmer. Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '26). DOI: 10.1145/3830398.3830522 This dataset provides a collection of 43,878 open legislative records from the Canadian House of Commons, spanning 1994 to 2025, covering document types such as debates (Hansard), legislative bills, committee reports, petitions, recorded votes, order papers, and Library of Parliament research publications. It is released at three stages of the same pipeline: the raw collected documents, a processed corpus that has been passed through an ETL pipeline and chunked for use in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, and an embedded, pre-indexed vector store built from that processed corpus. The dataset supports the development and user study of the InsightToast project. The embedded form can be placed directly into the project's codebase, open sourced at https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast, where it serves as the knowledge base when InsightToast operates as a proactive side-channel assistant in policy discussion meetings. Usage in the InsightToast Backend Only qdrant_storage.tar.gz is required to run the backend. Extract it into the root of the InsightToast project, so that qdrant_storage/ sits alongside docker-compose.yml, and start the services: tar -xzf qdrant_storage.tar.gz -C /path/to/InsightToast/ cd /path/to/InsightToast docker compose up --build -d Contents File What it is Approx. size parliament_data.tar.gz Raw source corpus of 43,878 parliamentary records, as 57,124 files (.txt + .pdf) 8.1 GB compressed / 11 GB extracted parliament_data_processed.tar.gz Processed corpus: the same records cleaned, normalized, and chunked into RAG-ready JSON 2.1 GB compressed / 9.1 GB extracted qdrant_storage.tar.gz Pre-indexed Qdrant vector store, ready to mount as the knowledge base 21 GB compressed / 27 GB extracted parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the raw corpus, viewable without downloading the archive small parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the processed corpus small qdrant_storage.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the vector store small SHA256SUMS.txt SHA-256 checksums for the three archives small Verify the archives after download: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt Source Corpus: Raw Parliamentary Documents parliament_data.tar.gz contains open legislative documents collected across the range of record types produced by the Canadian House of Commons and the Library of Parliament, including the proceedings of debate, the texts of bills as tabled, the reports of standing committees, the petitions presented to the House, and the recorded outcomes of divisions. The documents were assembled from three public sources: the House of Commons (ourcommons.ca, including the Legislative Information service, LEGISinfo), the Library of Parliament of Canada (parl-gc.primo.exlibrisgroup.com), and the independent open-data mirror openparliament.ca. No private, personal, or access-restricted material is included; Member of Parliament profiles contain only information published in an official public capacity. Total: 43,878 parliamentary records, distributed across 57,124 files (43,634 .txt + 13,490 .pdf). Each record is provided as extracted plain text, with the source PDF alongside it under the same basename where one exists, so records that carry both formats account for two files. Temporal coverage: documents span the 35th through 45th Parliaments. Debates run from 1994-01-17 to 2025-10-10; coverage of the other record types varies by type. Languages: the source records are bilingual (English and French), as published by Parliament. Filename conventions: debates use sitting dates (YYYY-MM-DD- .txt); bills, journals, order papers, and votes use - - (for example, 37-1-C-10); petitions and Library of Parliament publications use slugified titles. Processed Corpus: Cleaned and Chunked Records parliament_data_processed.tar.gz contains the same corpus after the ETL pipeline that turns each document into retrievable units. Documents are parsed from their metadata header and routed by document_type. Bilingual records are language-identified with langdetect and reduced to their English content by an LLM pass. PDFs are structurally partitioned with unstructured's partition_pdf into text, table, and image elements; table elements are linearized into prose by an LLM, and salient figures are captioned, written to images/, and linked from their chunk via has_images. Records whose content is inherently tabular, namely recorded votes, petitions, and Member profiles, are rendered into natural-language narratives to keep them semantically retrievable rather than reducing to fields. Type-specific pre-segmentation then splits debates on speaker turns, preserving the speaker, section, and timestamp, before every stream passes through a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (1,000 characters, 200 overlap); each resulting chunk is tagged with its content_type (text, table, or image) and its provenance. The output is one JSON document per record, holding the record's metadata and its ordered list of chunks: { "metadata": { "document_type": "debate", "session": "35-1", "date": "1994-01-17", "language": "en", "source_file": "debates/1994-01-17-1.txt", "source_url": "...", "total_chunks": 51 }, "chunks": [ { "chunk_id": 0, "content": "...", "metadata": { "speaker": "...", "section": "...", "content_type": "text", "has_images": false } } ] } Volume: 42,014 JSON records and 2,170 extracted images, totaling 6,379,732 chunks, which is the set embedded into the knowledge base below. Traceability: every record's metadata.source_file links back to its file in the raw corpus. Coverage: most record types are processed in full; committee-report and library are present as subsets of the raw corpus. See parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt for per-category counts. title: Renewal resetting of quantum dynamics: a classification for complete resets, a reduction for jump channels, and critical time scales

abstract: Unrefereed research candidate. A quantum system evolves under a fixed gate, step by step, and is occasionally reset; the waiting times between resets are independent and may have an infinite mean. Wald, Yao, Platini, Hooley and Carollo (Quantum 9, 1742, 2025, doi:10.22331/q-2025-05-13-1742) inferred from estimates and numerics how the averaged state behaves for the hazard r_n = gamma/(n+1)^alpha. This paper proves it: for alpha < 1 the state converges to a survival-weighted mixture, for alpha = 1 to the dephased state, and for alpha > 1 it approaches a rotating orbit and converges iff the reset state commutes with the gate. For complete resets the behaviour is classified for every renewal clock (finite mean, infinite mean, periodic, defective); a clock makes every finite-dimensional unitary reset system converge iff it is proper and aperiodic. This part is a short consequence of classical renewal theory. The claimed contributions are: the exact infinite-dimensional trace-norm defect 1 - m_pp (continuous spectral mass) for proper infinite-mean clocks, with no trace-norm convergent subsequence unless m_pp = 1; a laboratory-time reduction of imperfect resets (general jump channels, possibly noncommuting) to complete resetting at an effective state under a nonresonance condition (W), which is characterised, decidable for finitely supported clocks and open and dense, but is sufficient, not necessary, and not a classification; and uniform two-term asymptotics, endpoint and near-resonance crossovers for the critical clock gamma/(n+1), with practical time scales (dephasing can need more than 10^9 steps; numerical estimates).
